strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: zero-shot/plug-and-play high-definition video restoration using video consistency models, extending image-based latent consistency inverse solvers to video in a computationally efficient gradient-free Langevin framework.

The proposed product-of-experts combination of a video consistency model (for temporal causality/coherence), a frame-wise image consistency model (for spatial detail), and 3D total-variation regularization is conceptually reasonable and practically effective in the reported experiments.

The method requires few NFEs (7-9) and avoids backpropagation through the generative model, giving a significant memory advantage over autodiff-based video diffusion posterior samplers and making HD video restoration more feasible.

Evaluation includes challenging temporal/spatial super-resolution and temporal blur tasks at 1280x768, with strong improvements in FVMD and LPIPS over VISION-XL, plus qualitative evidence using spatio-temporal slices and videos.
The paper provides an ablation study and implementation details for the proximal steps, and the reported temporal-coherence gains over frame-wise image LDM baselines are meaningful.
weaknesses: The evaluation is narrow: only one dataset (Adobe240), only synthetic linear degradations, and no real-world video restoration benchmarks. The lack of a clear train/validation/test split is also concerning, especially since hyperparameters appear to be selected per problem via grid search.

Baseline comparisons are insufficient for a top-tier AI conference: only VISION-XL (frame-wise image LDM) and classical ADMM-TV. Video-aware diffusion/PnP inverse solvers are not compared, and excluding VDPS due to memory does not fully justify the absence of lower-resolution or alternative video-aware baselines.

The quantitative results are mixed: LVTINO improves perceptual/temporal metrics but has lower PSNR/SSIM than VISION-XL in multiple settings (Problems B and C). Claims such as state-of-the-art reconstruction quality are therefore stronger than the evidence supports.

The zero-shot/plug-and-play claim is weakened by using a task-specific joint deblurring/interpolation network to warm-start Problem C. This pretrained supervised model may inject significant prior information, and no ablation is provided to isolate its effect.

The theoretical justification for the product-of-experts prior with two different consistency models and two implicit likelihood half-steps is incomplete. Convergence guarantees are only cited under mild regularity assumptions and are not rigorously established for this multi-prior, multi-latent-space splitting scheme.

Algorithm 1 contains a likely bug: the condition `if k < N` is always true for k=0,...,N-1, so the final iteration never skips the ICM and second likelihood step, contradicting the text and the reported NFE count. The ICM noise sampling is also unclear (single latent noise broadcast across frames versus per-frame noise).

Reproducibility is limited: no code/models are released, compute details are minimal, prompt optimization is not explored beyond a generic prompt, and several design choices (e.g., mixed Adam/PDHG proximal solvers) are not fully justified.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: high-definition video restoration with generative priors, especially temporal consistency under severe spatio-temporal degradations.
Proposes LVTINO, a zero-shot/plug-and-play video inverse solver that integrates a video consistency model (VCM) with an image consistency model (ICM) and a spatio-temporal TV regularizer.
The gradient-free conditioning mechanism avoids backpropagation through large video diffusion models, which is a practical advantage over methods like VDPS in terms of memory.
Combines complementary priors: a VCM for temporal coherence and an ICM for per-frame spatial detail, which is a sensible product-of-experts design.
Provides experiments on high-resolution 1280x768 video and three difficult inverse problems, with visual slice analyses suggesting improved temporal continuity over VISION-XL.
Includes an ablation study (LVTINO-V) showing that a lighter VCM-only version can still be competitive with very few NFEs.
The paper is generally well written and clearly motivated, with useful background on DMs, CMs, and video diffusion models.
The method requires few NFEs relative to iterative diffusion posterior sampling methods, supporting its computational efficiency motivation.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the contribution is largely an integration of existing components (LATINO, VISION-XL, CausVid/Wan, DMD2, TV regularization, PnP Langevin sampling) rather than a fundamentally new inverse-problem or video-modeling advance.

The posterior sampling guarantee is weak and informal: the assumptions on the learned VCM/ICM priors are unlikely to hold in practice, and the Moreau-Yosida approximation plus the gamma << delta eta simplification is ad hoc and not rigorously justified.

The theoretical development does not establish convergence for the actual non-smooth, learned-prior Markov chain used in the algorithm; claims of approximate posterior sampling are stronger than the evidence.

Evaluation is narrow: only one dataset (Adobe240) is used, with short clips and synthetic linear degradations; no standard video restoration benchmarks (e.g., REDS, DAVIS, real-world video) are included.

Baseline comparisons are insufficient: only VISION-XL and ADMM-TV are compared. Other recent video inverse solvers, PnP video methods, frame-by-frame LDM baselines, and memory-efficient variants of video DPS are missing.
The omission of VDPS due to >80GB VRAM is understandable, but no smaller-resolution or memory-efficient comparison is provided, leaving a major class of diffusion posterior samplers unexamined.
Quantitative results do not consistently support the main SOTA claim: PSNR/SSIM is lower than VISION-XL on Problem B and PSNR is lower on Problem C, even though perceptual metrics improve.
Temporal consistency evaluation is limited mostly to FVMD; no optical-flow warping error, flickering metric, or human study is provided to substantiate the strong temporal-coherence claims.

For Problem C, the method uses an external joint deblurring/interpolation network (Shang et al.) for warm-start initialization. This is not counted in the NFE accounting and undermines the zero-shot/plug-and-play claim, as it introduces task-specific pretrained restoration.

The NFE accounting is misleading: applying the ICM across all frames is counted as a single NFE, but it still requires per-frame network evaluations, so the true computational cost scales with video length and is not fully reported.

Hyperparameters are chosen per problem via extensive grid search on the test metrics, raising concerns about overfitting to the evaluation; sensitivity to lambda, eta, delta, and schedules is not thoroughly analyzed.
The algorithm and notation contain inconsistencies (e.g., Algorithm 1 uses x_{k-1} rather than x_k in the VCM step; NFE schedules for VCM/ICM are not fully aligned), making reproducibility harder.
No code or model release is mentioned, and computational cost/runtime is not reported, limiting reproducibility and practical assessment.

The paper overstates its positioning (e.g., 'first' VCM-based inverse solver for HD video) and claims state-of-the-art reconstruction quality despite mixed quantitative results across metrics and problems.

strengths: Presents the first zero-shot/plug-and-play inverse solver for high-definition video restoration using video consistency models, directly addressing temporal inconsistency in frame-wise image-LDM solvers.
The gradient-free conditioning avoids backpropagation through large video diffusion/consistency models, reducing memory cost and enabling restoration at high resolution.

The method is theoretically grounded in Langevin posterior sampling with a product-of-experts prior, Moreau-Yosida regularization, implicit likelihood steps, and stochastic auto-encoder approximations.

Experiments on challenging high-resolution spatio-temporal super-resolution and blur problems show strong perceptual and temporal metrics, especially FVMD and LPIPS, with visual improvements over VISION-XL.
Provides useful implementation details, hyperparameter settings, and ablations comparing VCM-only and ICM-inclusive variants and different data-consistency schemes.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is incremental: LVTINO largely combines existing components, including LATINO-style Langevin sampling, CausVid/DMD2 consistency models, and 3D total-variation regularization.

Evaluation is limited to the Adobe240 dataset, with only VISION-XL and ADMM-TV as main baselines; comparisons to other video inverse solvers, diffusion posterior sampling methods, and simple frame-wise baselines are missing, and VDPS is omitted due to memory constraints.

Quantitative results are mixed: PSNR/SSIM are not consistently best, e.g., VISION-XL obtains better PSNR and SSIM on Problem B, so the claim of state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity is stronger than the evidence.
Ablation studies cover only Problems A and B, not the hardest Problem C; hyperparameters are tuned per problem, which raises questions about generalization and potential overfitting.
The computational advantage is modest: LVTINO uses 9 NFEs versus 8 for VISION-XL on Problems A/B, and the improved 7-NFE setting for Problem C relies on an external interpolation warm-start.

Theoretical assumptions about the validity of the product-of-experts prior, convergence under consistency-model approximations, and bias introduced by large step sizes and implicit proximal steps are not thoroughly validated.
Reproducibility is not fully established: code/data release details are absent, and several qualitative comparisons depend on external video links.

strengths: Introduces LVTINO, a zero-shot/plug-and-play inverse solver for high-definition video restoration that leverages Video Consistency Models (VCMs) as priors, extending the LATINO framework from images to video.

Provides a principled Bayesian/Langevin splitting scheme with a product-of-experts prior combining a VCM, an image consistency model (ICM), and a 3D TV regularizer; the resulting updates avoid automatic differentiation and require only a few NFEs (7-9).

Demonstrates clear improvements in temporal/perceptual metrics such as FVMD and LPIPS over VISION-XL on challenging video inverse problems, with strong qualitative evidence of reduced flickering and better motion coherence.
Includes useful ablations on data-consistency schemes, TV regularization, VCM-only variant, noise levels, and a non-linear JPEG restoration example.

Computational benefits are supported by runtime comparisons: fewer NFEs than iterative diffusion posterior sampling and faster wall-clock time than VISION-XL, while avoiding the prohibitive memory cost of backpropagating through a video diffusion model.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core algorithm is largely an adaptation of LATINO, replacing its image LCM prior with a VCM and adding a product-of-experts combination with an ICM and TV regularizer. The paper does not introduce a fundamentally new inference framework.

The central 'state-of-the-art' claim is not fully supported: on several settings PSNR/SSIM are lower than VISION-XL (e.g., Problem B on Adobe240 and Problems A/B on GoPro240), so the method mainly improves perceptual/temporal metrics rather than reconstruction fidelity across the board.

Measurement consistency is repeatedly claimed but not directly quantified; the evaluation does not report residuals such as ||y - A x_hat|| or noise-robustness diagnostics, which would be important for a PnP inverse solver.

The zero-shot claim is weakened for Problem C by using a supervised task-specific model (VIDUE) as a warm-start initialization. This makes the method less purely plug-and-play and complicates fair comparison with the baselines.

Evaluation is limited to a small set of baselines: mainly VISION-XL, ADMM-TV, and VIDUE. VDPS is omitted due to memory, concurrent work is not compared, and no error bars or statistical significance tests are provided.

Theoretical convergence claims rely on regularity assumptions on p_V and p_I (e.g., log-concavity/Lipschitz behavior) that are not verified for deep video/image consistency models; the practical approximation of the temperature parameter eta through timestep schedules is heuristic.

Reproducibility details for the VCM prior and its distillation/training (CausVid/Wan, DMD) are insufficiently specified, and the method still incurs high memory usage (~35 GB) despite being gradient-free.

Some presentation issues and inconsistencies remain, e.g., table-header typos/definitions for Problem A, unclear acronym usage, and incomplete details about how the VCM/ICM timesteps and hyperparameters were selected.

strengths: Proposes the first zero-shot/PnP inverse solver for high-definition video restoration using video consistency model (VCM) priors, extending the LATINO framework from images to video with a VCM+ICM+TV product-of-experts prior.
The conditioning mechanism is gradient-free and requires only a few NFEs, avoiding backpropagation through large video diffusion models and enabling experiments at 1280x768 resolution.
Provides extensive experiments on Adobe240 and GoPro240 across three inverse problems, plus ablations, runtime/memory measurements, noisy and non-linear JPEG experiments, and visual comparisons.
Achieves clear perceptual/motion improvements in several settings, especially LPIPS and FVMD, over VISION-XL and ADMM-TV, with visual examples of reduced flickering and better temporal coherence.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is largely an incremental combination of LATINO, an existing distilled video consistency model (CausVid/Wan), and standard TV regularization; the product-of-experts prior and alternating SAE/likelihood splitting are heuristic rather than fundamentally new.

Central claims are stronger than the evidence: LVTINO is not consistently state-of-the-art. PSNR/SSIM are often worse than VISION-XL, especially on GoPro240, and FVMD on challenging Problem C is worse than VIDUE in both datasets.

The Problem C evaluation is not a fair zero-shot comparison: LVTINO uses VIDUE, a supervised joint deblurring/interpolation network, to warm-start and reduce NFEs, then compares against VIDUE and zero-shot baselines. This undermines the plug-and-play/zero-shot claim and lacks an ablation without the supervised warm-start.

Baselines are limited: VDPS is excluded due to memory, DiffIR2VR is excluded due to unavailable checkpoint, concurrent zero-shot video restoration is not compared, and task-specific video inverse solvers beyond VIDUE are omitted. The comparisons are therefore insufficient to establish SOTA.

Theoretical justification is weak: convergence to the posterior is asserted via Laumont et al., but the implicit consistency-model priors do not satisfy the required regularity assumptions. The Moreau-Yosida approximation parameter gamma is not reported, and the splitting scheme is not rigorously shown to target the stated posterior.

Scalability/efficiency claims are not well supported: LVTINO uses more memory than VISION-XL (35 GB vs 15.6 GB for 25 frames), does not use the autoregressive VCM configuration, and does not demonstrate long-video restoration. It is also much slower than ADMM-TV.

Reproducibility and clarity issues: no code URL is provided despite the claim, key hyperparameters such as gamma are missing, and there are several inconsistencies/typos in tables and problem definitions (e.g., Problem A header, Table 5 vs. main Table 1, Problem B label in Table 7).

Ablations are incomplete: there is no ablation of the VIDUE warm-start, no analysis of posterior sampling quality beyond deterministic reconstruction metrics, and the VCM/ICM/TV contributions are not cleanly isolated in all settings.

Positioning relative to concurrent or flow-based PnP solvers is shallow: the paper does not sufficiently clarify what is fundamentally different from existing VCM/flow-based inverse methods beyond combining existing components.

strengths: Introduces LVTINO, the first zero-shot/plug-and-play inverse solver for high-definition video restoration using video consistency models as priors, with a clear and timely motivation.

Proposes a product-of-experts prior combining a video consistency model, a frame-wise image consistency model, and spatio-temporal TV regularization, integrated via a gradient-free Langevin splitting scheme.
Achieves strong perceptual and temporal-consistency improvements over VISION-XL, especially on FVMD and LPIPS, while using few NFEs and avoiding backpropagation through large video diffusion models.

Provides an extensive experimental evaluation on Adobe240 and GoPro240 at 1280x768 resolution, covering multiple spatio-temporal inverse problems (temporal SR + spatial SR, temporal blur + SR, joint SR).

Includes useful ablations and analyses: data-consistency scheme, TV regularization, VCM-only variant, hyperparameter sensitivity, scheduling choices, noisy measurements, non-linear JPEG restoration, runtime/memory, and qualitative video/slice comparisons.
Addresses a practically important limitation of frame-by-frame image LDM restoration: temporal flickering and incoherent motion, with clear qualitative and quantitative evidence.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is largely incremental over LATINO, extending an existing latent consistency inverse solver to video with a VCM/ICM/TV product prior and a custom splitting scheme.

The empirical gains are mixed: LVTINO does not consistently outperform VISION-XL in PSNR/SSIM, especially on GoPro240 and some Adobe240 problems, so the 'state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity' claim needs qualification.

Comparisons are somewhat limited: concurrent zero-shot video restoration methods such as Cao et al. (2026) are not included, and some relevant baselines are omitted due to unavailable checkpoints or memory constraints.
The method requires problem-specific hyperparameters (λ, η, δ, timestep schedules) and the ablation shows performance can degrade substantially under non-optimal configurations.
The evaluation is limited to relatively short 25-frame clips, and the paper does not demonstrate scaling to longer videos or autoregressive settings, which are important for video restoration.

Theoretical support for the full LVTINO sampler is limited: convergence guarantees are inherited/approximate and depend on assumptions about VCM/ICM priors, while the product-of-experts and TV steps are not rigorously analyzed.
Reproducibility is stated but not fully demonstrated, and exact replication may be challenging without released checkpoints/code and detailed implementation of the proximal solvers.
